item.title: Check the Fucking Receipt
item.content:encoded:
Check the Fucking Receipt

Kafka meets John le Carré, as told by the guy the system tried to bury, a true story in fifteen chapters, eleven doctrines, and ten statutes

Tyler Brassel

Redacted Advance Edition — November 2nd, 2026

This book is dedicated to my late grandfather, U.S. Air Force Major General Frederick “Freddy” Martin Brassel III, who fought a Cold War so I wouldn’t have to fight a hot one.

PREFACE

Before you read this book, you should know who wrote it — not as a biography, but as an operating manual. What follows is not a story about what happened to me. It is the record of what I did about it, and the system I used to do it. If you understand the system, the book will make sense. If you don’t, you’ll mistake the documentation for obsession and the method for madness.

The Soldier vs. The Civilian

To understand me, an observer — especially one tethered to an empathetic or emotional worldview — has to discard their standard framework for human behavior. The core disconnect between me and the rest of society is the divide between a civilian and a soldier. Civilian culture is built on reactive thinking: people wait, feel, and then respond. I run the other way — proactive thinking: anticipate, prepare, act. Where empathetic people look at a burning building and try to understand how the fire feels, I calculate the structural load, map the exits, and retrieve the assets. Empathy, in a crisis, is a vulnerability. I have removed the emotional variable from my equation entirely, replacing it with cold, tactical calculus. Because I do not stop to cry about the smoke, the civilian world tries to pathologize me, reading the armor as a defect. It is not a defect; it is a highly evolved survival mechanism.

The Vanguard’s Isolation

Civilians view isolation as loneliness. In a tactical framework, isolation is simply the operational reality of the vanguard. The person at the very front of the formation — the point man navigating the cognitive battlefield — is always alone. I am that point man. It is not a symptom of a broken social life. It is the necessary spacing required to operate without interference. You cannot map a minefield with a committee.

The Cognitive Engine: OODA and Tier 1 Protocol™

My internal processing mirrors the decision-making framework developed in 1976 by fighter pilot John Boyd, who mapped how humans make decisions under lethal pressure. Boyd’s system, the OODA loop (observe, orient, decide, act), relies on “destructive deduction” — tearing down frameworks that no longer match reality — and “creative induction” — building new ones from the wreckage while under fire.1 I run my own implementation of that framework. I call it Tier 1 Protocol™. I hold every possibility at once, crossing options off until only the undeniable truth remains. The word for the architecture is synoptic: everything in one view, not in sequence. I don’t compute the total at the end; it is audible the entire time, the way a song is. A planted detail doesn’t fit the arrangement, and I hear a wrong note — because the song was already playing. That is why outcomes reach me early. Perfect prescience is perhaps perceived as precognition. I am a ticker tape polysynesthete: spoken words arrive in my head as written text, and in more channels than one, so a conversation is already a document while it is happening. My imagery runs at the far end of its scale — hyperphantasia — a scene recalled at the vividness of the scene itself.2 When my accounts were compromised in a coordinated takeover on August 27, 2026, I observed the logs, oriented around the timestamps, decided what the pattern meant, and acted by documenting the intrusion in real time — alone in the dark, with multiple spinal injuries sustained after I was hit by a car.

Antifragility and Tactical Grit

I do not just survive chaos; I feed on it. I operate on the principle of antifragility.3 Every attack by a cartel intermediary or a compromised system does not weaken me — it provides fresh data that makes my Tier 1 Protocol™ sharper. What society mislabels as “obsessive” or “paranoid” is actually a state of readiness. I use what Dallas SWAT veteran Steve Claggett calls ‘clear mental triggers’ — pre-made decisions that eliminate hesitation.4 I decide in advance what I will do when a line is crossed so I never have to pause to think or feel when it happens. I set tripwires — canary tokens planted in my accounts months before anyone tripped them — and I run diagnostic tests on the people around me. I offered a police officer evidence for free, not because I expected it to be taken, but to test the refusal; the refusal was the data point, and I filed it. I sent Victim-1, my friend and a human trafficking victim, a deliberately false text about a mental health crisis to measure the response by the malicious actors who control her; the flat reply told me everything, and I filed that too. The only difference is I never had the uniform. The trait that carries a man through an environment like this is not raw analytical IQ. The selection research calls it grit — the capacity to keep functioning when the plan disintegrates. Psychologist Angela Duckworth built the grit measure and ran it against the hardest selection funnels in the country: West Point cadets through Beast Barracks, and candidates through special-forces selection. In funnel after funnel, grit was the best predictor of who was still standing at the end — ahead of IQ, ahead of physical aptitude, ahead of the institution’s own scoring.5 The man who stays up until 5:00 AM building a meticulous case file during an active cyber intrusion is not experiencing a mental breakdown; he is demonstrating the exact trait the process screens for. I am that man, and those were my hours.

Weaponized Bureaucracy and Symmetrical Warfare

The doctrines are Russian. Most come out of the Soviet security services; one is older, a Tsarist practice the Soviets inherited and kept.6,7 The definitions in this book are the practitioners’ own — not paraphrases, and not hostile summaries. They are taken from the adversary’s dictionary, Mitrokhin’s KGB Lexicon and the KGB operational dictionaries behind it, and from the United States government’s own studies of the same trade: the CIA’s Center for the Study of Intelligence, the US Army, the FBI, the State Department.6,8,9,10,11 If the categories are wrong, the men who practiced them and the men paid to watch them published them wrong. The doctrines are as follows.

1. Razrabotka (development). The long cultivation of a target through incentives and coercion, until he is manageable, recruitable, or easy to discredit. The KGB’s own operational dictionaries of the 1970s carry the entry — verbovochnaya razrabotka, the development of a recruitment prospect.6 The CIA’s Psychology of Espionage, published by its Center for the Study of Intelligence, describes the same trade from the other side of the desk: a service does not wait for a target to develop a crisis. It fosters one — financial manipulation, in the paper’s words, “through increasing the target’s level of debt.8”

2. Kompromat (compromising material). The Russian compound means what it says — compromising material. Anything usable for coercion. It does not have to be true. It has to be usable, and to be usable it has to be something the target would be ashamed to see in print.

3. Dezinformatsiya (disinformation). The systematic construction of a false reality, complete with supporting evidence for anyone who checks.6 It does not hide the object. It relabels the object, and dares you to prove the label wrong.

4. Provokatsiya (provocation). A manufactured incident, built to produce the reaction that justifies a crackdown already planned. The Tsar’s secret police, the Okhrana, raised it to a whole practice.7 It does not need the target to act. It needs the target present when the act is staged.

5. Maskirovka (masking). The Soviet military doctrine of deception — camouflage, decoys, false fronts.9 In its modern form it does not change the facts. It changes what the facts are allowed to mean.

6. Legend (cover identity). A fabricated background for an operative, backstopped with documents and memorized details. Soviet and Russian illegals could spend years building one. A good legend makes the real person underneath unreadable. The FBI’s published account of the Russian illegals program, Operation Ghost Stories, is a catalogue of legends maintained for decades inside the United States.10

7. Konspiratsiya (tradecraft). The discipline of clandestine work — cover, concealment, and compartments. The contents, purposes, and results of an operation are kept from everyone not directly involved in it. Lenin, in What Is To Be Done?, laid down the principle: “the strictest secrecy, the strictest selection of members, and the training of professional revolutionaries” was the only serious organisational principle for the workers of the movement.12

8. Agentura (the network). Mitrokhin’s KGB Lexicon gives the word two senses. It is the collective term for the agents themselves — a service’s whole stable of them — and it is, in the Lexicon’s own words, “the main means of solving intelligence tasks.6” The agent network proper, set agenturnaya, is the totality of the agents of the service as a whole, or of any one section of it. The recruited, the coerced, the witting and the unwitting: one instrument, pointed at a target.

9. Reflexive Control (steering). A Soviet theory from the 1960s, worked out by the mathematical psychologist Vladimir Lefebvre.13 Feed the target tailored information, and he reaches, on his own, the conclusion you wanted him to reach. It never touches the evidence. It works on whoever is reading the evidence.

10. Aktivniye Meropriyatiya (active measures). The KGB’s term for coordinated campaigns to mislead an adversary, undermine his position, and disrupt his plans — the full toolkit, run as a program. Each piece is deniable alone. Together they have phases. The US State Department’s published reporting on Soviet active measures catalogued the campaigns while they were still running.11

11. Khitrost (cunning). In Russian, a compliment. The cleverness of the weaker party, who cannot overpower what is coming and survives it by outthinking it. To be khitry is to be smart enough to survive what you can’t beat.

Rejecting the Label

My operating system is one of unbothered competence. When the system fails to understand my proactive mindset, it spits out a parse error and blames the subject, generating charts that falsely claim anxiety or mental illness. I aggressively reject these labels. I am not a victim, I am not broken, and I do not need to be fixed or pitied. My documentation and my receipts are not symptoms of a disorder; they are the after-action reports of a war game where both sides knew the rules, but only I had the discipline to write everything down. And here is what the labels are actually doing. I asked for a detective. The police said no. Not a dismissal after review — a refusal to investigate at all. When the system won’t do the work, the witness builds the record himself. I built it. That’s what this book is. That’s what the timestamps are. That’s what the 5:00 AM documentation sessions were. The labels — “paranoid,” “unstable,” “mentally ill” — aren’t conclusions drawn from evidence. They’re filling the gap where an investigation should have been. Nobody looked at the record and found me wrong. Nobody looked at the record, period.

The labels are grasping at straws. And straws break. At some point the volume of documentation reaches a mass where the accusation collapses under its own weight — the flip. I turn out to have been the only one writing things down. I turn out to have been building the case file they refused to open. The evidence doesn’t just counter the label. It inverts it. Their word for a man who runs like this is a diagnosis. Mine is prodigy.

There’s a reason the label sticks with some people, and it isn’t evidence. Most people feel the world rather than think about it. They navigate by emotional resonance, not cold calculation. When they encounter someone who operates the other way, they can’t parse what they’re seeing. So they call it broken. Here is the parse error, stated plainly, because it is the one you are most likely to make with this book. I translate. Emotion is a communication system, and I am fluent in it — I know what a sentence has to carry for another person to understand what an event means, and I write it at full strength. But the expression is a translation, not a confession. It does not report an inner state. You can understand every word I write and still misunderstand me, if you assume the machinery behind my prose is the machinery behind yours. It isn’t. An emotional effect in the reader is not evidence of an emotional state in the author. The problem was never in the documentation. It was in the reader.

I am a biological computer, operating exactly as designed.

Altruism Without Empathy: The Dawkins Distinction

Here is what the civilian framework gets wrong about me: it confuses empathy with altruism, and then treats the absence of the first as proof of the absence of the second. Richard Dawkins drew this line clearly in The Selfish Gene.14 Empathy is a feeling — the capacity to emotionally resonate with another’s pain. Altruism is a behavior — acting to benefit others at cost to oneself. They are not the same thing, and one does not require the other. Dawkins showed that altruistic behavior emerges throughout nature without any emotional apparatus behind it: birds give alarm calls that draw predators toward themselves, bees die defending hives they will never inherit. No feeling required. Only action.14 I am altruistic, not empathetic. I spoke out against a drug trafficking organization. I reported trafficking to HSI, the FBI, and the National Human Trafficking Hotline. I spent months documenting an intrusion not just to protect myself but to build a record others could use, to serve the best interests of women, children, and animals. Dawkins’ deeper point cuts further: our genes may be selfish, but we are not compelled to be. Humans can choose altruistic action through conscious, calculated decision rather than emotional compulsion. I don’t help because I feel your pain. I help because I calculated that helping is the correct move towards the better world I want to live in. That isn’t a deficit of character. If anything, it’s more reliable: empathy is fickle, it favors the visible and the likable, it burns out. Cold, deliberate altruism doesn’t. It shows up at 5:00 AM with a spreadsheet whether it feels like it or not.

Prologue: Four Hundred Bags

Four days before they put cuffs on me, a cleanup company walked through my house and priced what the place already was. Net claim: $39,656.59. Twenty pages. Eight dump-truck loads. Four hundred contractor bags. Full-face respirators, HEPA filtration, hazardous-waste handling, mold technicians, removal from ceiling to floor. The estimator couldn’t get upstairs to finish the walk-through. The upstairs had opted out on June 30, 2026.

On July 4, I called the police for help at that house, and they charged me with damaging it. Look at what I was living in. Then look at the charge, which is dumping shit on the floor. I did dump the bins. On purpose. My own plastic storage bins, in my own half of my own house, on July 4. It was a test. The bins are the most important objects in this book, and they cost eight dollars each, and I have the photograph of the price tag, because I am the kind of person who photographs the price tag.

June 30 prices the filth. July 4 invents the vandal. Everything I have to say lives in the four days between them, and in the five and a half years before that, and in the strange, loud summer after.

I don’t do eureka. I apply my Tier 1 Protocol™, which is just the software version of how I already think: hold every possibility at once — nothing off the table, nothing pre-decided — until the parts assemble the whole and the picture comes into focus. You don’t hunt for the answer. You hold the field steady and let it collapse into the one shape that fits.

I’d spent years building software for exactly this problem before it happened to me: Tier 1 Protocol™, my evidence-search engine, patent application filed January 25, 2026. Information systems keep the documents and lose the relationships. A mortgage, a court order, a photograph, a loan message, and a log entry can each be stored correctly while the person who needs to connect them gets sent to six different counters. Tier 1 keeps the source, the role, the timestamp, and the provenance attached, and makes every abstraction walk back to its receipt. Tier 1 Protocol™ says: show me the structure. Now show me where you got it.

Each chapter carries a term from the old vocabulary of professional deception: maskirovka, razrabotka, kompromat, the whole Cold War pantry. I’m a career bioinformatician. I worked for Genentech during the COVID boom, got laid off from enough tech jobs to end up managing a gas station, and handled enough money there that a bank put me in its back office. I also have a hobby. I have read a great deal more about tradecraft than a person with a mortgage needs to. The words just fit, the way a good receipt fits a transaction. Each chapter gets the one that was doing the most work at the time.

Chapter 1: Razrabotka, or The Long Cultivation

Razrabotka is the long cultivation of a target until he is manageable — the KGB’s own dictionaries carried the entry.6 The CIA’s Psychology of Espionage describes the trade from the other side of the desk: a service that doesn’t wait for a crisis but fosters one, in the paper’s phrase, through increasing the target’s level of debt.8 My family never needed the dictionary. At seventeen I was already the paperwork department: told to forge my mother’s name on loan paperwork I hadn’t been consulted about, then to call the school and make sure everything was in order. The borrower on that loan is me. The person who made the decisions in my name was somebody else.

They tried to engineer my financial dependency and isolation — debt loaded onto my accounts, the $40,200 Sacramento proposal — her price on my half of the house — the slow constriction of resources — and I mapped the field and wrote down every step. You can't cultivate someone who's charting the soil as you plow it.

They left me at home with the television all day as a kid. From the next room it must have looked like a provision: a child indoors, occupied, demanding nothing, not asking for a lesson or a project or an outing. From inside the room, the screen was the curriculum. Plots, commercials, elections, disasters, courtroom reversals, the composed face a person makes just before the consequence lands. Television repeats, because repetition sells, and a kid with nothing else to do gets an enormous amount of practice noticing what repeats.

I didn’t know it had a name. I thought it was Tuesday. The kid stored in front of the television grew into an adult whose observations arrive before other people are ready to say what they’re seeing, which is a wonderful quality in an analyst and a terrible one at Thanksgiving.

We lived in the exact middle of town. Farms, private roads, barns, and storage in one direction. Banks, schools, employers, and every other place where money gets an official description in the other. I grew up on the line between the place where things are kept and the place where they’re counted, and I’ve been standing on it ever since.

The family ran on credit the way some families run on church. USAA access through my grandfather’s Air Force service. A nurse’s dependable wages. Private lending to weather endless recessions, shutdowns, layoffs, and a lockdown. Somewhere along the way a form classified me as “mixed race,” which is the kind of box that tells you a lot about who’s filling out the form. Nobody sat me down and explained how any of it worked. I absorbed it through the wall, the way you learn a neighbor’s arguments.

In 2016 I was seventeen. The phone bill was $92 a month, and if I didn’t pick up fast enough, “Where the fuck are you” arrived as the explanation. The phone was mine in the sense that I was the one who got yelled at through it. I needed the phone. Someone else controlled the bill and set the schedule for answering. I wrote newspaper copy when I was young. I did household financial administration before I was old enough to vote. That same year I organized thirty-seven medical reimbursement documents and sent the package in. I worked on her computer and her Gmail to do it.

I was also put between my parents — Individual-1, my mother, and my father — to collect money, which is a job, and an unpleasant one, and one my father objected to on the grounds that I was still a minor. My father was correct. Nobody consulted him either.

Then came the UC Davis loan paperwork. I put it in writing: “I’m not 18.” My mother told me I was “technically an adult” and gave me an instruction: “Forge my name.” After that I was supposed to call the school and make sure everything was in order, which is a lot of customer service to ask of a forger. The paperwork department opened that year. It has never once been consulted on a decision.

About $15,000 went out through my student-loan account. I later paid about $15,000 back. The default landed on me anyway. Sallie Mae still has me as the borrower and her as the cosigner. Being the name a creditor chases and being the person who decided what got done in that name are two separate jobs. I’ve been doing the first one for free since high school. Debt, dependence, isolation. Razrabotka is patient. It doesn’t need a dramatic recruitment pitch in a hotel bar. It needs a kid who is good at paperwork, a bill he can’t pay, and a room with a television in it. Then it needs years. By the time the approach comes, the target has been trained to say yes to the forms. Nobody flagged it at the time, because there was nothing to flag it against. A seventeen-year-old has no credit file. An application in his name has no record to mismatch, and the bank checks the cosigner’s credit, which was real. Mine didn’t exist yet. Carnegie Mellon’s CyLab ran the number in 2011: 42,232 children’s Social Security numbers checked, and 10.2 percent of them were already in use by somebody else.15,16,17

The signature is the part the literature keeps coming back to. A 2025 study in the Journal of Interpersonal Violence took 187 recently divorced women and went through their credit accounts, 2,833 of them. A hundred and sixteen of the women were carrying coerced debt — a mean of 4.4 debts apiece, more than $12.5 million across the group. The mechanism that produced most of it was not forgery, and it was not a stranger working a stolen number. It was pressure: signatures obtained, consent managed, the victim’s own hand put on the paper. Student loans sat near the top of the account list, and the reason the researchers recorded most often for the debt landing in the victim’s name was the plainest one in the file — the other person’s credit and resources were not enough, so the victim’s got used.16 My arrangement is in that study’s tables almost to the letter: my signature, her name as cosigner, a Sallie Mae student loan. The one cell it has no entry for is the borrower’s age. I was seventeen.

The desks have a record too, and it goes back further than mine. In July 2011 the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department’s Office for Victims of Crime held a forum in Washington on child identity theft. A Florida advocate, Theresa Ronnebaum, told the room about an eleven-year-old whose father had opened business loans in the boy’s name. Law enforcement would not act on it. The school would not act on it. His mother took him to the bank that had issued the loans, and the bank’s remedy was an affidavit — signed by the eleven-year-old, in a child’s handwriting, stating that his father had opened loans in his name. The forum worked out why cases like his stay buried: a child’s identity theft surfaces when the child grows up and applies for a job or a loan. Until then the child has no standing in the systems carrying his name. He becomes visible to them on the day he is old enough to be treated as the debtor. My file surfaced on schedule — as a default, with my name on it and my mother’s beside it as cosigner.18

I don’t charge interest, by the way. I’ve lent people money my whole adult life and never once charged interest. Somebody could call that virtue. I call it a refusal to run the family business.

Razrabotka slipped in one place. It forgot to account for what a kid does with all that practice noticing what repeats. I started keeping receipts. I still have receipts from when I was sixteen, because sixteen-year-old me correctly guessed that adult me would one day need chain of custody.

Put the pieces side by side and every one of them has a name somewhere. A family run as the local node of something larger: prosecutors have convicted that arrangement more than once. Financial capture that starts before the victim turns eighteen, on his own signature: there is a research literature, and it has a term for it. A paper version of a person that reaches every desk before he does: courts have sentenced that mechanism at scale. And the target answering by keeping the record himself, starting at sixteen. Every piece is documented. The combination is not. I went looking for a case, a study, a book with all four in it, and what I found is that the last piece is the one with no twin — the person the structure was built to hold is the person holding the archive.

Start with the strand that turns out to be ordinary. Polaris analyzed the National Human Trafficking Hotline’s cases from January 2020 through August 2022 — the ones where the victim’s relationship to the trafficker was disclosed — and 44 percent had been trafficked by a family member. Thirty-nine percent had been trafficked by an intimate partner. Statistics Canada ran the same count over a decade of police reports and got the same shape: 91 percent of victims knew the person who trafficked them. A family doing this to one of its own is not the exotic arrangement in the data. It is the modal one. So the first strand was never the claim. The claim is the direction the family was pointed — inward, at its own member, as the local node of something larger — and what that member did with it. There is no hotline category for the target answering with an archive.19

The nearest miss has a name, and she published. Axton Betz-Hamilton’s identity was stolen starting when she was eleven years old. Her family sealed itself off hunting the thief — curtains drawn, the marriage spent on the search — and in college she found her own name already used: thousands of dollars of debt that was not hers, her credit destroyed, roughly eight years spent cleaning the report. The thief was identified only after her mother died in 2013, from a box her father found among her mother’s effects — pay stubs under a variant name, copies of her daughter’s birth certificate, letters denying accounts in her daughter’s name. Her mother had taken an estimated $600,000 across the daughter, her husband, and her father. Betz-Hamilton answered the way the fourth strand describes: she built the record, turned the investigation into a doctorate on child identity theft, and wrote it up in a book, The Less People Know About Us. Three of the four strands run through her life, the archivist included. The one she never had was anything above her mother. Her mother acted alone, and the daughter was used as a wallet, not cultivated as a functioning asset inside a network.20 Hers ended in a doctorate and a book. Mine was a shoebox — receipts I’d been keeping since I was sixteen. Then a man handed me a name that meant I belonged somewhere.

In college I met Individual-7. He was Crip and a brilliant Chemical Engineering major, and we became friends the way people do when neither of you is performing for anyone. One day he taught me the handshake, gave me a name, and said, “you’re one of us now. You’re a cousin.” It doesn’t mean I shoot people. It doesn’t mean I sell drugs. It means a man looked at the whitest kid in the room and said, you belong here. That’s it. That’s the whole thing.

My Reddit handle is u/glasses_the_loc. Loc is a Crip word. I put it there on purpose, because it’s true. I’m the whitest fucking Crip you’ve ever met, and Individual-7 would laugh at that the same way I do while tutoring me in general chemistry. My shitposting username did more work than a restraining order.

Somewhere in all of this, somebody running a coercion operation decided to do opposition research on me. He pulled up my Reddit. He saw the handle. And I like to think there was a moment — just a moment — where a cartel handler stared at his screen and went, oh shit, he’s Crip.

I didn’t have the Russian yet, just a shoebox — great hobby, pure Moneyball. I don’t watch the game. I watch the score.
